newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaraguans cheered by U.S. halt to deportations.
newsitem.headline: Nicaraguans cheered by U.S. halt to deportations.

text.p: Nicaraguans rejoiced on Thursday in reaction to a U.S. federal court ruling that immediately halted the deportation of 14,000 Nicaraguans living in the United States.

U.S. District Judge James Lawrence King in Miami told government lawyers on Wednesday "no one will be deported," at least until Nicaraguan claims the United States has improperly denied them residency status can be heard.
"This is a positive sign," Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Sandra Montenegro told Reuters. "All Nicaraguans view this as a very good signal and we are very content."
U.S. Justice Department officials said no decision had been made on a possible appeal, but one official privately said she assumed the decision would be appealed.
Many of the immigrants affected by the ruling fled Nicaragua during a civil war in the 1980s that pitted the former leftist Sandinista government against U.S.-armed Contra rebels.

Any mass deportation would be a blow to the weak Nicaraguan economy. Nearly 60 percent of the workforce is unemployed or underemployed, and remittances from Nicaraguans abroad are a major source of foreign currency.
Reaction from the office of President Arnoldo Aleman was delayed by a transport stoppage and other protests led by the leftist Sandinista Front, now the major opposition party.
The judge's ruling dominated Nicaraguan newspaper and radio coverage. "Nica immigrants triumph," read the banner headline in La Prensa.
"We are very content. We're heading down the right path," Cristobal Mendoza, president of the president of the Committee of Poor Nicaraguans in Exile, told the pro-government newspaper La Tribuna.
Nicaragua's television Channel 8 broadcast live from Miami a news conference with Mario Lovo, one of the lawyers representing the Nicaraguans in the class-action suit.
Lovo told reporters in Miami that the ruling "portends victory in the future," adding the judge recognised the "irreparable harm that they would face if they were deported."
Lovo said some 40,000 Nicaraguans eventually could benefit from the ruling, about half of them war refugees.

"Of course we are happy," street vendor Antonio Rosales, who said he depends on the $120 a month that his sister sends from Miami, told the state-owned Radio Nicaragua. "It's a big break, and we hope that this can be resolved definitively."
